That's why Bill Haley's cover changed many lines.
nl: In 1954, Bill Haley and the Comets signed with Decca and covered two blues songs: Rock Around the Clock, first recorded by Sunny Dae in 1952, and Joe Turner's Shake, Rattle and Roll.
Joe Turner, 1911 to 1985, had sung jazz since the late twenties, both slow jazz blues and faster jump blues, and was called a blues shouter, because he matched his voice to the honking saxophones.
In his own words, he put swing to the blues and made the blues jump.

His Shake, Rattle and Roll, from 1954, is a twelve bar blues at about 140 beats per minute, with boogie woogie piano, a bass on all four beats, hand claps and snare drum accenting the backbeats, and a jazz style baritone sax solo.
It ends with a saxophone line taken from Duke Ellington's Take the A Train.
His lyrics are full of sexual references, like the couple being in bed together and the sun shining through her dress.
It was number one on the rhythm and blues charts for three weeks, but never made the pop charts.

n: Shake, Rattle and Roll, by Bill Haley and His Comets, 1954.
Rock and roll, from a former western swing bandleader.
Haley's version is faster and cleaned up for white radio audiences.
Listen for the slapped country bass, and the saxophone and guitar playing the riff together instead of a jazz solo.
items.lyr: The same basic complaint, but the sexual lines are removed: instead of being in bed, she's told to get out of the kitchen, and instead of revealing dresses she's cold and treats him wrong. The "one-eyed cat" line stayed, probably because most listeners wouldn't catch the joke.
nl: Haley's version is faster, at about 176, with fewer jazz characteristics.
The piano and drums play a shuffle, the bassist slaps the strings against the fingerboard in the country style, and the backbeat is less obvious.
Instead of an improvised solo, the sax and guitar play the melody together.

The references to the bed are removed, and the lines about her sexuality are changed to lines about her being cold and treating him wrong, though Haley probably kept the one eyed cat line because it was subtle enough to slip past easily offended listeners.
Haley's version reached number seven on the pop charts.

n: Rock Around the Clock was number one on the pop charts for eight weeks and number three on the rhythm and blues charts.
It's a twelve bar blues with uneven beat subdivisions, except in the guitar solo, and saxophones playing riffs rather than jazz improvisations.
The lyrics use the word rock to mean dancing and partying, but young listeners knew the blues singers' use of rock as slang for sex.

It wasn't a big success in 1954, but became a hit after it was used as the title music of the 1955 movie Blackboard Jungle, and because the movie was about teen rebellion, the thirty year old Haley and his band came to stand for that attitude.

Their 1957 tour of Britain made them the first international rock stars, but their mix of western swing and rhythm and blues proved less lasting than rockabilly, the combination of honky-tonk country and rhythm and blues.
Sam Phillips, 1923 to 2003, an Alabama farm boy who worked as a disc jockey in his teens, moved to Memphis in 1944 and opened the Memphis Recording Service.
He loved the blues and recorded mostly African American blues musicians from the South, including Jackie Brenston's Rocket 88, Howlin' Wolf, Rufus Thomas, and Junior Parker.
First, Rufus Thomas.
Junior Parker, with his song Mystery Train.

Phillips's business was too small to distribute records nationally, so he sold many of his early recordings to larger companies like Chess, until he formed the Sun Record Company in 1951 to release them himself.

Phillips knew that white teenagers were increasingly interested in rhythm and blues, but that they tended to buy records by white artists, and that radio programmers wanted sexual references kept out of lyrics.
What he needed was a white singer who could capture the style and beat of African American singers, while adapting the lyrics to white tastes.
He found him in 1954, when the young Elvis Presley, 1935 to 1977, came into the studio to record My Happiness and That's When Your Heartaches Begin as a birthday present for his mother.
Elvis's Sun recordings introduced American teenagers to rockabilly, a name made from rock and hillbilly.
The band was just an electric lead guitar, an acoustic rhythm guitar, a string bass, and subdued drums.

Guitarist Scotty Moore played with an even country beat on some songs and uneven picking on others, sliding notes up the strings to imitate a steel guitar, while Elvis kept the rhythm on acoustic guitar.

Bassist Bill Black slapped the strings against the fingerboard, a sound typical of rockabilly, while the drums played a rhythm and blues shuffle with accented backbeats, and Phillips added reverberation that exaggerated the throbbing pulse.
Some of Elvis's early songs came from the blues and some from country.
One of his first singles had the blues song That's All Right, by Arthur Big Boy Crudup, on one side.
First, Crudup's original.
Now Elvis's version.
The other side was a rockabilly version of the country song Blue Moon of Kentucky, by the bluegrass writer and performer Bill Monroe.
First, Monroe's original.
Now Elvis's version.
After some local success, Phillips sent Elvis to audition for the Grand Ole Opry, but he was rejected, because his style was too black for the Opry and too white for rhythm and blues audiences.
In fact, his voice had no direct precedent in either tradition: a wide, syrupy vibrato suggesting warmth, which could suddenly shift into a falsetto suggesting bottled up tension and wildness.

He was clean cut and good looking, in James Dean's rebel image, and although he sang cleaned up versions of sexually suggestive blues songs, he put sex into his performances with suggestive poses and hip gyrations.

His Sun recordings, such as Good Rockin' Tonight and Milkcow Blues Boogie, follow the twelve bar blues form, but at faster tempos than blues or rhythm and blues, and that speed gave rockabilly its energetic intensity.
In 1955 he was still seen mainly as a country singer, and Arthur Godfrey's Talent Scouts turned him down in New York.

When Colonel Tom Parker became his manager, he decided Elvis needed a bigger company than Sun, and after his recording of Junior Parker's Mystery Train drew attention, RCA bought his contract for just thirty five thousand dollars, a deal that wasn't necessarily a mistake for Phillips, since Elvis needed more publicity than Sun could afford.
For purist rockabilly fans, his Sun recordings are better than his RCA ones.
At RCA, under Parker's aggressive management, Elvis became a star within a year.

He wasn't a songwriter, and many of his RCA songs came from pop writers, recorded with a clean studio sound, doo-wop style backup vocals, and Fats Domino style piano, though rockabilly was still used sometimes, as on Blue Suede Shoes.
It was his irresistible performance style that earned him the title King of Rock and Roll.

In 1956, he sang Heartbreak Hotel, I Want You, I Need You, I Love You, Don't Be Cruel, and Hound Dog on the Milton Berle, Steve Allen, and Ed Sullivan shows, thrilling teenage girls and angering their parents, and Ed Sullivan showed him only from the waist up.
Hound Dog, by Willie Mae Big Mama Thornton, 1952, written by Leiber and Stoller.
Rhythm and blues.
Thornton was a powerful blues singer, and her version was number one on the rhythm and blues charts for seven weeks.
Listen for her rough, commanding voice, the bluesy guitar bending notes, and the very strong backbeat from claps and drums.
items.lyr: A woman throws out a man who has been cheating on her and living off her. In African American slang, a "hound dog" is a man who chases other women. "Wag your tail" mocks him like a begging dog; she's done feeding him.
nl: Hound Dog was written by the songwriting team of Leiber and Stoller for Willie Mae Big Mama Thornton, who recorded it first, in 1952.
In African American slang, a hound dog was a man who cheated on his woman, and Thornton sings it to such a man, vowing to stop seeing him.

In the listening guide, her version is a twelve bar blues at about 140, sung in a rough classic blues voice, with country blues guitar fills bending into blue notes, and hand claps plus a drum hit on its shell for a very strong backbeat.
It was number one on the rhythm and blues charts for seven weeks in 1953, but never made the pop charts.

n: Hound Dog, by Elvis Presley, 1956.
Rock and roll.
Elvis's version was number one on the pop charts for eleven weeks, and it changes the meaning of Thornton's song.
Listen for the faster tempo, the drum hits on the backbeat, the country style guitar solo, and the backup singers holding long chords.
items.lyr: The lyrics were changed: now it's a man insulting someone as worthless, like a hound dog that "ain't never caught a rabbit," a useless hunting dog. "You ain't no friend of mine" and claims of being "high-classed" become lies he sees through. The cheating-man meaning of the original is gone.
nl: Elvis's 1956 version changes the meaning, berating a woman as no more useful than a hound dog that can't catch rabbits, which fit his tough guy image.

It's faster, starting at about 176 and speeding up, with country style guitar, a bass riff modeled on the saxophone riffs in Bill Haley's Shake, Rattle and Roll, drums heavily accenting the backbeat, and backup singers sustaining chords.
Backed with Don't Be Cruel, it was number one on the pop charts for eleven weeks and on the rhythm and blues charts for six.

n: Elvis became a movie star with Love Me Tender in 1956, and each movie was followed by a string of hits.
With his check from Sun he bought his parents Cadillacs, and in 1957 he bought Graceland, where his mother's pink Cadillac stayed parked, since she never learned to drive.
His 1957 movies, Loving You and Jailhouse Rock, featured the hits Teddy Bear and Jailhouse Rock.
In 1958, while he was filming King Creole, he was drafted into the army, and soon after he left for basic training his mother died, which he called the worst loss of his life.
Parker kept fans' attention during his two years of service by releasing songs Elvis had already recorded, such as Hard Headed Woman and A Big Hunk o' Love.
Burning Love, by Elvis Presley, 1972.
Rock.
This was Elvis's last top ten hit, from his later career.
Listen for the strong backbeat, the mix of straight and swung rhythms, and the backup singers breaking into black gospel style at the end.
items.lyr: He's so full of love and desire that he feels like he's on fire: burning, his temperature rising, flames licking at his body. "A hunk, a hunk of burning love" means a big piece of passion. It's playful exaggeration, not a story.
nl: After the army, Elvis was more a movie star than a concert performer, until he returned to touring, TV specials, and Las Vegas shows from 1968 on.

His rough rockabilly style was long gone, and country fans felt he had sold out to pop, but his ability to follow trends kept him popular for three decades, and his fifties image influenced so many performers that he became a living legend.
Buddy Holly once said that without Elvis, none of them could have made it.
The listening guide is his last top ten hit, Burning Love, from 1972, which reached number two on the pop charts.

At about 144 beats per minute, it mixes even and uneven subdivisions, with the bass and guitar even, the piano and Elvis's vocals uneven, a strong backbeat on the drums, and a backup group that breaks into black gospel style at the end.
The lyrics: he's so full of desire that he's burning up.

In his last years, his wife Priscilla divorced him, and he lived as a recluse at Graceland, renting whole stores and theaters at night to avoid his fans, and his dependence on prescription drugs contributed to his death in 1977, at forty two.

n: Blue Suede Shoes, by Carl Perkins, 1956.
Rockabilly.
Perkins was a Tennessee singer, guitarist, and songwriter at Sun Records, and this song was number one on the country charts and number two on pop and rhythm and blues.
Listen for the stop time openings, where his voice is alone except for hits on the beat, the slapped bass, and the drummer playing on the rim.
items.lyr: You can do anything to me: knock me down, burn my house, steal my car, drink my liquor. Just don't step on my new blue suede shoes. The shoes stand for a young man's pride and style. The opening ("one for the money...") is a traditional children's countdown before a race, and "cat" is slang for a cool guy.
nl: Carl Perkins, 1932 to 1998, grew up on a farm in Tennessee and played guitar at country dances.
He loved the blues and rhythm and blues, and after hearing Elvis on the radio he modeled his style on Presley's and was signed by Sun in 1955.
Unlike Elvis, he wrote songs and played lead guitar, and Phillips let Elvis go partly because he thought Perkins might be an even bigger star.
His career was launched by his own song, Blue Suede Shoes, in 1956, which was number two on both the pop and rhythm and blues charts and number one country.
In the listening guide, it's a twelve bar blues based song at about 168 beats per minute, with some choruses stretched to sixteen bars.

Most choruses begin with stop time, the voice alone with the band joining only on the beats, and the band is hollow body electric guitar, acoustic rhythm guitar, slapped stand up bass, and drums played on the rim.
The singer values his blue suede shoes, and dancing in them, above everything else in his life.
On the way to The Perry Como Show, where he was to receive a gold record for the song, Perkins was badly injured in a car accident that killed his brother Jay and his manager.
By the time he recovered, rockabilly was fading, though he went on to a successful country career.

n: The Beatles paid tribute to Perkins by covering several of his songs, and in the sixties and seventies he performed with Johnny Cash and Bob Dylan.
In 1983, Paul McCartney featured him on his album Tug of War.
The early eighties rockabilly revival band the Stray Cats took much of their style from Perkins.
He overcame throat cancer in 1995 and kept writing and recording until his death three years later.
Jerry Lee Lewis, 1935 to 2022, was a pianist and singer whose rock career was short but influential.
He grew up in Louisiana listening to country and blues, and as a cousin of the preacher Jimmy Swaggart, he was also influenced by gospel.
After hearing Elvis's Sun records, he went to Memphis and signed with Sun.
Like Haley and Elvis, he covered blues songs by African American musicians, and his Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On, from 1957, had first been recorded by Big Maybelle in 1955.
First, Big Maybelle's original.
Unlike Haley and Presley, Lewis didn't clean up the sexual lyrics, and even added to them.
He played honky-tonk piano rock with tremendous energy, his right hand sweeping across the keys in glissandos, meaning sliding runs, while his left hand pounded out a pumping bass line.
On stage he kicked away the bench, played with his feet, and even jumped on top of the piano, earning the nickname The Killer.
Bruce Springsteen said of him that he doesn't play rock and roll, he is rock and roll.

His career was ruined by an unofficial boycott when the public learned he had married his thirteen year old third cousin without divorcing his second wife, and as he put it, going from ten thousand dollars to two hundred fifty a night was a hell of a disappointment.
He stayed at Sun recording country music, but could no longer draw large crowds.
In 1973, the British rock musicians Rory Gallagher, Alvin Lee, and Peter Frampton had him join them for an album called The Session.
First, Rory Gallagher.
Alvin Lee, with his band Ten Years After.
items.s: I'd Love to Change the World

n: Peter Frampton.
From the late seventies into the nineties, Lewis played his old hits on tribute programs, and in 1995 he released a new album, Young Blood.
Rockabilly was first created in Elvis's Sun recordings, but the fusion of blues and country was so natural for the time that other artists soon copied it.
Eddie Cochran, 1938 to 1960, had a short career but a lasting influence.

Originally from Oklahoma, he lived in Minnesota and California before settling in Nashville, where he wrote songs with his friend Jerry Capehart, and he adopted the tough guy image of James Dean and Marlon Brando, even acting in the 1957 movie Untamed Youth.
His hits came from experiments with overdubbing, where he played and sang all the parts himself.
Overdubbing was invented by Les Paul in the early fifties, and Cochran was among the first rockabilly musicians to use it extensively.
First, Les Paul with Mary Ford.
Summertime Blues, by Eddie Cochran, 1958.
Rockabilly.
Cochran was a young rockabilly star who played and sang every part on this record himself, through overdubbing.
Listen for the instrumental breaks between his lines, and the deep voice he uses to play the boss, his parents, and a congressman.
items.lyr: A teenager complains about his summer: he has to work, and when he asks his boss for time off, the boss says no. His parents won't let him use the car because he didn't work late. He even writes to his congressman, who says he's too young to vote. "Raise a fuss, raise a holler" means complain loudly, and "there ain't no cure for the summertime blues" means nobody will help him.
nl: Cochran's biggest hit was Summertime Blues, number eight on the pop charts in 1958.
In the listening guide, at about 152 beats per minute, it alternates A and B sections, and Cochran overdubbed the lead vocals, acoustic rhythm guitar, string bass, hand claps, and drums.
The repeating rockabilly rhythm has four even beats with a double accent on both halves of the second beat, and instrumental breaks draw attention to parts of the vocal line.
The singer is in agony because, when he should be having fun, everyone is making him work.

n: His next hit, C'mon Everybody, from 1959, also came from his overdubbing experiments.

Cochran saw rockabilly dying with the rise of teen idols in the late fifties, and his last hit, Three Steps to Heaven, wasn't rockabilly at all, but had a lightly strummed guitar, a doo-wop style vocal group, and very little bass, drums, or backbeat.
He never got to establish his new style, because he was killed in a car accident on his way to a London airport after a tour of England in 1960.
Gene Vincent, 1935 to 1971, was with Cochran on that tour and survived the accident.
He grew up in Virginia singing a religious country style called white gospel, served in the navy during the Korean War, and then formed a rockabilly group called the Blue Caps.
Capitol Records signed them, seeing his voice as competition for Elvis, and used an echo effect to imitate the Sun sound.
Be-Bop-A-Lula, from 1956, was their first recording and his biggest hit.
His image was rougher than Elvis's, and because a navy leg injury kept him from Elvis's hip movements, he conveyed sexual desperation through breathy vocals instead.
Lotta Lovin' was a hit in 1957, but by then rockabilly was losing popularity in the United States.
Instead of switching to pop, Vincent moved to England and kept performing rockabilly, until he returned to America in poor health in 1971 and died within a month.
Charles Hardin Holley's last name was misprinted without the e early in his career, and he kept it that way.
Buddy Holly, 1936 to 1959, from Lubbock, Texas, played fiddle, guitar, banjo, and piano as a child, and turned to rock after seeing Elvis perform in 1955.

In 1956 he recorded country songs for Decca in Nashville that didn't sell, so he and his drummer, Jerry Allison, went back to Texas, formed the Crickets, and recorded their first hit, That'll Be the Day, in 1957 in New Mexico, produced by Norman Petty.
Holly was no Elvis imitator: he wrote much of his own music, his witty, personal style appealed to men as well as women, and his light voice had a trademark hiccup.
Instead of the leather jackets of rockabilly rebels like Cochran and Vincent, he wore suits, ties, and horn rimmed glasses, a clean cut look that Elvis Costello would later portray as neurotic.
Elvis Costello, who later borrowed Holly's look.
Peggy Sue, by Buddy Holly, 1957.
Rock and roll.
Holly was a singer, guitarist, and songwriter from Lubbock, Texas, and one of the first rock guitarists to play a solid body electric guitar.
Listen for the nonstop tom tom drumming, the hiccups in his voice, and the guitar solo suddenly bursting out louder.
items.lyr: A simple love song: if you knew Peggy Sue, you'd understand why he loves her so much. He repeats her name and says she's pretty, and that he longs for her. The word play and repetition matter more than any story.
nl: The Crickets used the standard rockabilly lineup of lead guitar, rhythm guitar, bass, and drums, but their guitars were electric, and Jerry Allison played a more important role than other rockabilly drummers, sometimes using Latin rhythms.
Apart from their stand up bass, the Crickets had the same lineup as many later groups, including the Beatles and the Rolling Stones, both of which covered Holly's songs.
Holly was one of the first rock guitarists to play a solid body electric guitar, whose more aggressive tone soon made it the standard rock guitar.
The listening guide is Peggy Sue, from 1957, number three pop and number two rhythm and blues, which combines blues and country characteristics.
It's a twelve bar blues at about 148 beats per minute, with an electric guitar, acoustic rhythm guitar, string bass, and drums playing an energetic pattern on the tom toms with little or no backbeat.
Holly strums quietly during the verses, then plays a louder strummed solo influenced by Chuck Berry, and his vocal hiccup is clearest in the later choruses.
The Crickets' rhythm guitarist said he didn't play on the recording, so Holly may have overdubbed the rhythm guitar himself.
The song is about his unrequited love for a girl named Peggy Sue.

n: Late in 1958, Holly left the Crickets and their manager, Norman Petty, married, moved to New York, and began changing his style toward the new pop trend.
His last hit, It Doesn't Matter Anymore, was written for him by the songwriting teen idol Paul Anka and recorded with an orchestral string section.

Because his money was tied up in legal battles with Petty, Holly went on one more concert tour, backed by a band that included guitarist Tommy Allsup and bassist Waylon Jennings, who later became a country star.
The other headliners were the Big Bopper, Ritchie Valens, and Dion.
First, Waylon Jennings.
The Big Bopper, whose real name was J.P.
Richardson.
Ritchie Valens, born Richard Valenzuela.
Dion, Dion DiMucci.
The Big Bopper, Valens, and Holly all died in a plane crash on February third, 1959, a date rock fans have never forgotten.
The Everly Brothers, Don and Phil, were one of the few country influenced rock groups to stay popular from the late fifties into the early sixties.
Their parents were country musicians with a radio program, on which the boys performed from 1946, at nine and seven years old.
Their closely harmonized tenor voices were accompanied by their own rhythm guitars, lead guitarist Chet Atkins, pianist Floyd Cramer, bass, and drums.
Their sound was smoother and fuller than Sun rockabilly, without the slapping bass, and their voices slid up to high notes, sounding almost on the verge of tears.
They signed with Cadence Records in 1957 and recorded many of their best known songs, including Bye Bye Love and All I Have to Do Is Dream.
First, Bye Bye Love.
All I Have to Do Is Dream, from 1958.
items.s: All I Have to Do Is Dream

n: In 1960 they moved to Warner Brothers and recorded their biggest hit, Cathy's Clown.
Their later sales didn't match their early records, and after a fight on stage in 1973 they broke up, reuniting ten years later, but their vocal style influenced many singers.
Now their sidemen, starting with the lead guitarist, Chet Atkins.
Floyd Cramer.
The book ends the chapter with a box on early electric guitars.
An acoustic guitar has a hollow body with a sound hole, so the vibrating strings make its top, the soundboard, resonate.
Early jazz guitarists like Charlie Christian and T-Bone Walker played hollow body guitars with two f shaped holes and electric pickups attached, such as the Gibson E S 150.
First, Charlie Christian.
Urban blues guitarists wanted more punch than a full hollow body gave, so they chose thinner, semisolid guitars, like B.B.
King's Gibson E S 335, which he affectionately named Lucille.
Les Paul and others were bothered by the short sustain and occasional feedback of semisolid guitars, and improved their pickups until the whole body could be made of solid, dense wood.
While Les Paul was still working on his model, Paul Bigsby built one that Merle Travis played in 1947.
Leo Fender created the Broadcaster, later called the Telecaster, in 1948, and Gibson released the Les Paul model in 1952.
Buddy Holly played a Fender Stratocaster, first produced in 1954, an improvement on Fender's earlier models with three pickups.

The Telecaster, the Les Paul, and the Stratocaster all became standard instruments for sixties rock guitarists, such as Eric Clapton, who played a Les Paul, and Jimi Hendrix, who played a Stratocaster.
First, Hendrix on his Stratocaster.
To recap chapter four.
Rock clearly began in blues and rhythm and blues, and the name rock and roll was first used for rhythm and blues.

By the fifties, new styles had emerged that were something more: blues and gospel based music by African American artists such as Fats Domino, Chuck Berry, and Little Richard, who added country and other influences, and blues songs covered by country musicians such as Bill Haley, Elvis Presley, and Buddy Holly.
However we label it, this fifties rock is the music on which the rest of rock history is built.
End of chapter four.
Before chapter five, the book introduces the decade of the sixties.
The decade began with optimism under the young new president, John F.
Kennedy, who promised to beat the Soviet Union in both the missile gap and the space race, and set the goal of putting a man on the moon by the end of the decade, a goal reached in 1969.

His fight against communism had setbacks: the failed Bay of Pigs invasion of Cuba in 1961, and the Cuban missile crisis, which he resolved, but only after bringing the world closer than ever to nuclear war.
He was assassinated in 1963, after only about a thousand days in office.
The civil rights movement grew underneath that optimism.

In 1960, four African American college students sat down at a whites only Woolworth lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, and were refused service, and within two weeks these peaceful sit-ins had spread across the country.
Violence followed too, with riots in fifty eight cities between 1964 and 1967, the worst in Watts in Los Angeles, Newark, and Detroit.
Doctor Martin Luther King worked to keep protests peaceful, while Malcolm X warned of a powder keg about to explode, and both men were assassinated, Malcolm X in 1965 and King in 1968.

There were also legal victories: the Twenty-Fourth Amendment of 1964 outlawed poll taxes, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned discrimination in most public places, King's 1965 march from Selma to Montgomery led to the Voting Rights Act, Thurgood Marshall became the first African American Supreme Court justice in 1967, and the 1968 Housing Act outlawed discrimination in housing.
The Vietnam War was the most controversial issue of all.

Presidents Truman, Eisenhower, and Kennedy sent advisers and then troops to keep South Vietnam from communist takeover, and President Johnson escalated with more troops and bombing, at first with wide public support.

By 1966, veterans' reports of destroyed villages, wasted aid, and soldiers returning with drug problems, along with rising casualties, turned many Americans against the war, leading to protests on college campuses and young men avoiding the draft, while others still saw it as a necessary fight against communism.
The war continued until Saigon fell in 1975, and returning veterans received little support.

Other movements began as well: Rachel Carson's 1962 book Silent Spring warned about pesticides like DDT, and Betty Friedan's 1963 book The Feminine Mystique launched the women's liberation movement, attacking the idea that women belonged only at home and the practice of paying men more for the same work.
The hippie movement rejected mainstream society, with psychedelic drugs, beads, and headbands as its symbols.

Much of its optimism ended with the drug related deaths of Jimi Hendrix and Janis Joplin in 1970 and Jim Morrison of the Doors in 1971, and with a killing at the Rolling Stones' Altamont festival in 1969.
First, Jimi Hendrix.
Janis Joplin.
Jim Morrison, with the Doors.
The Rolling Stones, whose 1969 Altamont festival ended in violence.
Chapter five: Teen-Styled Rock Music.
By 1960, most of the strongest performers of mid fifties rock had stopped performing, leaving no competition for the lighter pop rock that emerged between 1957 and 1960.

Carl Perkins stayed out of music after his 1956 car accident, Little Richard entered the ministry, Jerry Lee Lewis's records were banned over his marriage to his young cousin, Elvis Presley was in the army, and Chuck Berry was on trial under the Mann Act and later went to prison.
Buddy Holly, the Big Bopper, and Ritchie Valens died in the 1959 plane crash, and Eddie Cochran was killed in the 1960 car accident that badly injured Gene Vincent.

Some of these performers had already sensed that pop was the future: Presley was recording more pop than rockabilly at RCA, and Holly's It Doesn't Matter Anymore and Cochran's Three Steps to Heaven were pop songs.
Rockabilly artists who refused to change, like Gene Vincent and Ronnie Hawkins, left to perform in England and Canada, where rockabilly was still popular.
Here's Ronnie Hawkins.

Payola means paying for airplay or other publicity, and some form of it existed as far back as the Civil War, when vaudeville performers agreed to sing a song at every show in return for having their photo printed on its sheet music.
By the late fifties, payola meant paying radio and television programmers to play particular songs, so that money, rather than quality, decided what got played.

It wasn't illegal until after the scandal, but it was considered unethical, and small independent labels depended on it, paying for airplay in one town and using the profits to do the same in the next.
The scandal was set off by songwriters, or rather by their representatives.

The Copyright Act of 1909 gave songwriters three ways to be paid: a share of sheet music sales, mechanical fees for each piano roll or recording sold, and performance fees whenever the song was performed in public.

The American Society of Composers, Authors, and Publishers, known as ASCAP, was formed in 1914 to collect performance fees from concert halls, clubs, restaurants, and other venues, and distribute them to its members.

ASCAP generally excluded blues, rhythm and blues, country, and rock writers, so in 1940 broadcasters who resisted ASCAP's fees and monopoly formed Broadcast Music Incorporated, or BMI, which most rock writers of the fifties and early sixties joined.

As rock's popularity cut into its profits, ASCAP looked for ways to discredit the music BMI handled, and in 1958 it asked a congressional committee, already investigating cheating on TV quiz shows, to look into bribes paid to disc jockeys.
That investigation became the payola scandal, and many small labels that had depended on payola for airplay went out of business.
Disc jockey Alan Freed, 1921 to 1965, had fought racism by giving African American artists as much airplay as he could, but he had also accepted a lot of payola.

By then he had his own ABC television show, Dance Party, and although ABC asked him to deny the charges, evidence like his name appearing as a co-writer of Chuck Berry's 1955 hit Maybellene made his guilt obvious.
He pleaded guilty, lost his show, was also convicted of income tax evasion, and died in 1965 as his drinking worsened.
Another disc jockey investigated in the scandal, Dick Clark, 1929 to 2012, escaped ruin.
He hosted the teen dance show American Bandstand, which brought Philadelphia pop music and dances to teenagers all over the country.

It occasionally featured rockabilly and rhythm and blues artists, but much more often clean cut, white teen idols such as Pat Boone, Paul Anka, Frankie Avalon, Connie Francis, Fabian, Bobby Rydell, Brenda Lee, and Bobby Vee, while the leather jackets and rebellious messages of rockabilly had no place there.
Clark did have financial interests in some of the records he promoted, but he was cleared when his lawyers showed he also promoted records he had no stake in.
He had to sell his music business interests but kept his show, largely because the industry saw American Bandstand as a positive influence on teens, while Freed's music was seen as corrupting.

Television brought rock into homes in other ways too: Ed Sullivan added rock performers to his Sunday night family show to attract teenagers, and by 1965 ABC had the prime time rock show Shindig and NBC had Hullabaloo.
We'll hear most of those teen idols later in the chapter.
First, Bobby Vee, who isn't discussed further.
items.s: Take Good Care of My Baby

n: Tutti Frutti, by Little Richard, 1955. The original, to compare with the cover that follows.
It reached number seventeen on the pop charts and number two on the rhythm and blues charts.
Listen for his growling, no holds barred vocal with octave leap oohs, the jazz style walking bass, and the drummer's strongly accented backbeat.
items.lyr: Twelve bar blues form, with stop time breaks where the voice is alone. He sings about rocking with Sue (rocking was slang for sex) and hints that Daisy knows how to love him too, so he may not be true to Sue.
nl: Most teen idols, especially the men, sang in the style of the crooners of the twenties through the forties, such as Perry Como and Bing Crosby.
Pat Boone, born in 1934, became popular singing pop ballads as well as covers of blues and rhythm and blues songs.
He changed those songs differently than the rockabilly singers had, because he wasn't after rockabilly's energy, and his recordings fit his clean cut, boy next door image.
While Carl Perkins and Elvis dared anyone to step on their blue suede shoes, Boone's trademark was clean white buck shoes.
The book compares Little Richard's original Tutti Frutti, which reached number seventeen pop and number two rhythm and blues, with Boone's cover, which reached number twelve pop.
Little Richard's version, from 1955, is a twelve bar blues at about 172 beats per minute.

It opens with a two bar introduction of nonsense syllables that shows off his no holds barred vocal style, punctuated by leaping oohs, and the last four bars of some choruses are sung over stop time breaks.
The piano plays even subdivisions against the uneven beat, with a jazz style walking bass, saxophone punctuations, and a strong backbeat on the drums.
In the lyrics, rocking with Sue was slang for sex, and Daisy knows how to love him too, hinting that he isn't faithful to Sue.
First, Little Richard's original.

n: Tutti Frutti, by Pat Boone, 1956.
Teen idol pop, a cover of Little Richard.
Boone was a clean cut, boy next door crooner, famous for his white buck shoes, and his version reached number twelve on the pop charts, higher than the original.
Listen for how he imitates Little Richard's rhythmic phrasing without his growl, the smoother and more polite voice, and the weaker backbeat.
items.lyr: Same twelve bar blues form and almost the same tempo. Boone removed the sexual references: no rocking, and instead of having two girlfriends he admits Daisy tempts him but stays true to Sue. He said he changed words that seemed too raw for him.
nl: Pat Boone's version, from 1956, is slightly faster, at about 176 beats per minute.
He imitates Little Richard's rhythmic singing and inflections, but without his growl, and his voice sounds smoother, more controlled, and polite.
A backup group sings ahs, the beat subdivisions are uneven throughout, the backbeat is less obvious, and the only jazz touch left is the tenor saxophone solo.
Boone removed the sexual references: there's no rocking with Sue, and instead of having two girlfriends, he admits Daisy tempts him but stays true to Sue.
Boone said he changed some words because they seemed too raw for him, and Little Richard joked that white kids put Pat Boone's record on the bed and hid his in the drawer.

Many rock fans would say Boone wasn't a rock singer at all, but the book argues his Tutti Frutti counts as rock because of its historical context: it represents the pop direction rock followed for the rest of the fifties and into the sixties.

n: Movies and television supported the clean teen idol image.
Pat Boone played teenagers in the movies April Love, in 1957, and Journey to the Center of the Earth, in 1959.

Once American Bandstand was broadcast nationwide, it introduced the Philadelphia teen idols Frankie Avalon, Fabian, and Bobby Rydell, who were then promoted further by movies such as Beach Blanket Bingo, starring Frankie Avalon and Annette Funicello, a former Mouseketeer from The Mickey Mouse Club.
We'll hear Avalon and Rydell with songs the book names later.
First, Fabian, whose real name was Fabian Forte.
Annette Funicello.
Ricky Nelson, 1940 to 1985, was more important to rock for his rockabilly recordings, but his appearances on his parents' TV show, The Adventures of Ozzie and Harriet, gave him a teen idol image.
Two of the most successful female singers of the teen idol era were Connie Francis, born Concetta Franconero, and Brenda Lee, born Brenda Mae Tarpley.
We'll hear Connie Francis with a song the book names later.
First, Brenda Lee.
Most teen idols succeeded more through their looks and how much teenagers identified with them than through musical talent.
Their natural but untrained voices captured youthful enthusiasm, and on TV, in movies, and even in live shows they usually lip synced to their records.
They rarely played instruments beyond some simple guitar chords, and they generally didn't write songs.

Paul Anka, born in 1941, was the exception: he wrote many of his own hits, as well as hits for others, including It Doesn't Matter Anymore for Buddy Holly, My Way for Frank Sinatra, and She's a Lady for Tom Jones, along with the theme music for Johnny Carson's Tonight Show.
First, Frank Sinatra's My Way.
Tom Jones, with another Anka song.
Venus, by Frankie Avalon, 1959.
Teen idol pop.
Avalon was one of the Philadelphia teen idols introduced on American Bandstand, and Venus was number one for five weeks.
Listen for the very full production with orchestra, chorus, and drums, and the gentle, sincere mood of his crooning.
items.lyr: He is so desperate for romance that he prays to Venus, the Roman goddess of love, for a girlfriend, but he is also choosy and lists exactly what she should be like. A typical teen idol theme: puppy love and dreaming of the perfect mate.
nl: Teen idol songs were as youthful and wholesome as the singers' images, mostly about the ups and downs of puppy love and dreams of the perfect mate.

Examples include Frankie Avalon's Venus, from 1959, Connie Francis's Where the Boys Are, from 1961, Paul Anka's Puppy Love, from 1960, and, on other teenage concerns, Bobby Rydell's Swingin' School, from 1960.
The listening guide is Venus, number one on the pop charts for five weeks.
It's at about 114 beats per minute, in A A B A form with an eight bar introduction of oohs from a chorus, and a full production with orchestra, chorus, and drums.
The mood is gentle and the singer very sincere.
In the lyrics, he's so desperate for romance that he prays to Venus, the Roman goddess of love, for a girlfriend, though he's also quite picky and lists exactly what he wants.

n: Connie Francis.
Paul Anka.
Bobby Rydell.
Because it featured teenage dancers, American Bandstand started or spread many dance crazes of the late fifties and early sixties.
In the fifties, teens danced the bop to songs like Gene Vincent's Be-Bop-A-Lula and Dance to the Bop, and Danny and the Juniors' At the Hop.
Variations on the bop took animal names, like the Pony, the Chicken, and the Monkey, while the Dog and the Alligator were considered too suggestive for American Bandstand.
First, Gene Vincent's Dance to the Bop.
Danny and the Juniors.
In 1960, a young Philadelphia performer named Ernest Evans covered a song called The Twist, by the blues singer Hank Ballard.
For his stage name, he chose Chubby Checker, a not so subtle variation on Fats Domino's name.
First, Hank Ballard's original.
Chubby Checker's version did more than become a hit: it started a dance craze that lasted several years, with more Twist songs by Checker and others, including the Isley Brothers and Sam Cooke.
Checker's songs also popularized other dances, such as the Pony, the Fly, and the Limbo.
The Isley Brothers.
Sam Cooke.
Latin music is part of the history of American popular music, though Latin rhythms influenced jazz much more than rock.
One Latin rock hit was by the teen idol Ritchie Valens, 1941 to 1959: La Bamba, from 1959, based on a traditional Mexican dance song.
Since pop singers rarely wrote songs, the pop boom created a need for specialized songwriters.
Many pop hits between 1959 and 1963 were written and published in the Brill Building, at 1619 Broadway in New York, or across the street at Al Nevins and Don Kirshner's Aldon Music Company.
Their songs combined influences from gospel, doo-wop, and teen idol music.

Most of the writers worked in teams, the most famous being Howard Greenfield and Neil Sedaka, Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil, Doc Pomus and Mort Shuman, Gerry Goffin and Carole King, Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller, and Jeff Barry and Ellie Greenwich.
Sedaka, Mann, and King were also performers who sang some of their own hits.
First, Neil Sedaka.
items.s: Breaking Up Is Hard to Do

n: Barry Mann.
A song by Doc Pomus and Mort Shuman, recorded by the Drifters.
items.s: Save the Last Dance for Me

n: Carole King, singing one of her own songs.
items.s: It Might as Well Rain Until September

n: The writer and producer George Shadow Morton worked with Jeff Barry and Ellie Greenwich to create short storyline songs, unusual for pop, such as Remember, Walkin' in the Sand, and Leader of the Pack, both sung by the Shangri-Las in 1964.
First, Remember.
Leader of the Pack.
Female vocal groups such as the Andrews Sisters had been popular from the mid twenties on, singing mainly swing jazz and later adding other styles, including gospel.
Will You Love Me Tomorrow, by the Shirelles, 1960.
Brill Building pop, by a girl group.
It was written by Gerry Goffin and Carole King, and the Shirelles, unusual for the time, also wrote some of their own songs and had twelve top ten hits in four years.
Listen for Shirley Alston's lead backed doo wop style by the other Shirelles, and the orchestral strings playing the fills and the instrumental section.
items.lyr: AABA song form. The singer plans to sleep with her date and is unsure the relationship will last beyond that night. Carole King said it spoke for young women facing the double standard of the time: will you respect me in the morning?
nl: In early sixties popular music, women were still mostly singers rather than instrumentalists, and trios and quartets of female singers, known as girl groups, became popular with teens.
The Shirelles placed twelve top ten hits on the pop charts between 1960 and 1963, and, unusually for pop singers of the time, did some of their own songwriting.
The listening guide is their first number one hit, Will You Love Me Tomorrow, from 1960, written by Carole King and her then husband, Gerry Goffin, a good example of the Brill Building pop sound.
It was number one pop for two weeks and number two rhythm and blues.
At about 138 beats per minute, in A A B A form with even subdivisions, Shirley Alston's lead is backed by the other Shirelles in doo-wop style.
The drums stress the backbeat with two quick notes on beat two and a single accent on beat four, and orchestral strings play fills at phrase endings and the lead in the instrumental section.
The singer plans to sleep with her date and isn't sure the relationship will last beyond that night.

Carole King said the song spoke for young women wondering whether they should or not, and whether he'd still respect them in the morning, cutting to the heart of the sexual double standard of the time.

n: Phil Spector, 1940 to 2021, was a Brill Building writer and producer whose productions were so distinctive that his style became known as the wall of sound.
He used so many instruments, overdubbed and mixed so thoroughly, that they formed a massive wall of instrumental color behind the vocals.
He disliked stereo, because it separated instruments from each other.

When he did let a single instrument stand out, the effect was colorful, as in the Spanish flamenco style guitar fills on the Crystals' Uptown, from 1962, or the natural sound of rain behind the Ronettes' Walking in the Rain, from 1964.
First, the Crystals.
The Ronettes, with Walking in the Rain.
A standard rock drum set wasn't enough for Spector.

He loved classical music, especially the nineteenth century German romantic composer Richard Wagner, and imitated Wagner's colorful use of percussion, adding chimes, castanets, triangles, timpani, and gongs to an already full sound.
His records didn't sound Wagnerian, but they had more orchestral fullness than earlier rock records that used only strings or brass, and he called them symphonies for teens.
Songwriter Ellie Greenwich said his records had a Wagnerian power and intensity, and that everything got bigger and bigger until there was no more record.
Here's Wagner himself.
Spector worked in both New York and Los Angeles, and started his own company, Philles, named for Phil and Lester Sill, who handled the business until Spector took full control late in 1962.
He often owned his groups' names as well as the singers' contracts, so he could use any combination of singers and call them the Crystals, or Bob B.
Soxx and the Blue Jeans.
He presented Darlene Love, whose real name was Darlene Wright, with an unnamed backup group that could change from record to record.
First, Bob B.
Soxx and the Blue Jeans.
items.a: Bob B. Soxx & The Blue Jeans

n: Darlene Love.
items.s: (Today I Met) The Boy I'm Gonna Marry

n: Be My Baby, by the Ronettes, 1963.
Girl group, produced by Phil Spector.
Spector's wall of sound overdubbed so many instruments, mixed together in mono, that they blend into one massive background, and he called his records symphonies for teens.
Listen for Ronnie singing the verses alone, the other two answering be my baby in the refrains, and the strings, guitars, keyboards, brass, saxophones, and percussion piled up behind them.
items.lyr: She promises her lover undying love and affection for all eternity, and asks him to be her baby. Spector later married Ronnie, the lead singer.
nl: The one group Spector kept as a regular trio was the Ronettes, and he married their lead singer, Ronnie Bennett, in 1967.
The listening guide is Be My Baby, from 1963, number two pop and number four rhythm and blues.
At about 132 beats per minute, its wall of sound comes from overdubbed strings, guitars, several keyboards, brass, saxophones, and many percussion instruments.
The three Ronettes don't harmonize: Ronnie sings the verses alone, and the other two answer with be my baby in the refrains.
Low strings play the melody in an instrumental section, and a short break punctuated by percussion separates the third and fourth refrains.
In the lyrics, she promises her love and affection forever.

n: Spector kept his reputation for hit records, and was asked to sift through hours of tape by the soon to disband Beatles, add backing, and produce their album Let It Be, recorded in 1969 and released in 1970.
George Harrison and John Lennon both had him produce their solo work, including Harrison's All Things Must Pass and The Concert for Bangladesh, and Lennon's Imagine.
First, the Beatles.
George Harrison, from All Things Must Pass.
John Lennon.
In the mid seventies, Spector tried a comeback producing Cher and Dion, but couldn't recapture his earlier success.
First, Dion.
Cher.

In 1980, he produced the Ramones' album End of the Century, giving the punk band a sound strikingly different from their earlier records, which wall of sound fans liked and most longtime Ramones fans considered a disaster.
His 1991 boxed set was titled Back to Mono, stressing how important mono recording was to his thick sound.
In 2009, Spector was sentenced to nineteen years to life in prison for the shooting death of the actress Lana Clarkson.
items.s: Do You Remember Rock 'n' Roll Radio?

n: While East Coast pop rock was about puppy love and teen dances, West Coast musicians developed their own danceable style, surf rock.

Surf vocals weren't based on the crooner tradition, and surf bands played their own instruments instead of using studio orchestras, in some ways a return to older rock played on guitars, bass, and drums, though the image and sound were light and pop oriented.
Instrumental hits were more common in surf rock than in any earlier style, with saxophones and electric organs, but mostly electric guitar, in the lead.
The surf guitar style was built on three sources: Duane Eddy, the Ventures, and Dick Dale.
Duane Eddy, born in 1938, created a style called twangy guitar by plucking the strings very close to the bridge, where they are tightest, for a strong, nasal attack.
He played repeated lead lines on the guitar's bass strings, with vibrato and studio or amplifier echo, giving a constantly wavering sound that may have reminded surf groups of moving water.
John Fogerty called him the first rock and roll guitar god.
His first hit, Rebel-'Rouser, from 1958, has the energy of gospel music and an instrumental call and response, in which a saxophone answers his guitar.
His next hits were Ramrod, a blues, and Forty Miles of Bad Road, in a standard pop song form.

The Ventures, from Tacoma, Washington, were one of the most important early instrumental groups associated with surf, although they only adopted the surf image after other surf groups had copied them.
They had two guitarists, an electric bassist, and a drummer, with a sound clearly influenced by Duane Eddy's twang.

They were one of the few surf groups to keep their following through the sixties and beyond, recording a version of the theme for the TV show Hawaii Five-O in 1969, and thanks to a large following in Japan, they were still popular when surf music was revived in the United States in the early eighties.
Dick Dale, born Richard Anthony Monsour, 1937 to 2019, was called the King of Surf Guitar, because he created a style copied by many surf groups of the early sixties.

Originally from Boston, he was living in Balboa, California, when his band, Dick Dale and the Del-Tones, began with Duane Eddy's twangy style, as in Let's Go Trippin', from 1961, a blues in form but not in style.
Misirlou, by Dick Dale and the Del Tones, 1961.
Instrumental surf rock.
Dale, the King of Surf Guitar, turned a Greek melody into a showpiece using the tremolo technique of Middle Eastern plucked instruments, which his Lebanese uncle taught him.
Listen for the very fast up and down picking that sustains each note while his other hand slides along the neck, and the amplifier reverb that gives the guitar a wet, surf sound.
items.lyr: No lyrics, only some wordless background vocals. The melody is broken up and varied to show off the guitar. Near the end the rock backbeat drops out for a Middle Eastern rhythm. A slower version was used in the film Pulp Fiction in 1994.
nl: In his version of the Greek melody Misirlou, also from 1961, Dale developed a technique based on the tremolo of Middle Eastern plucked string instruments, meaning very fast repetitions of a note.
As his Lebanese uncle had taught him, he picked a string up and down very fast while sliding his other hand along the fingerboard, creating an impressive effect of speed, and added Eddy's twang.
In the listening guide, at about 192 beats per minute, the form is through composed, meaning the melody is broken up and varied rather than repeated in sections.
It opens with an unmeasured guitar introduction of fast tremolo picking and rapid descending scales, and amplifier reverb gives the guitar a wet sound, like being in the surf.

n: Other instrumental surf groups that followed Eddy, the Ventures, and Dale included the Marketts, the Chantays, and the Surfaris.
Their hits often took titles from surfing: the Chantays' Pipeline, from 1963, is named for the curled shape of a wave, and even skateboarding sidewalk surfers knew what the Surfaris' Wipe Out meant.
Surf performances often had very active drum solos with crashing cymbals, imitating waves crashing on the beach.

The Beach Boys were formed in Hawthorne, California, by three brothers, Brian, Carl, and Dennis Wilson, their cousin Mike Love, and a neighbor, Alan Jardine.
The Wilsons' father, Murry Wilson, managed them, and after the success of Surfin', from 1961, he got them a contract with Capitol Records.

They were more than a surf group from the start: guitarist Carl Wilson used Eddy's twang and Dale's tremolo, but also imitated Chuck Berry's riffs, and Brian Wilson, the main writer and producer, based the group's vocal harmonies on the jazz vocal group the Four Freshmen.
Brian Wilson said that when he first heard the Four Freshmen's Day by Day, he loved the sound, and learned all his harmonies from them.
Sweet Little Sixteen, by Chuck Berry, 1958.

It reached number two on the pop charts and number one on the rhythm and blues charts, and the Beach Boys later reused its music for the next song.
Listen for Berry's guitar riff running through the song, the boogie woogie piano with long glissandos in the instrumental section, and the breaks where his voice is alone.

The Beach Boys' 1963 hit Surfin' U.S.A. had the same melody, chords, and form as Chuck Berry's 1958 hit Sweet Little Sixteen, and although Wilson first claimed the writing credit, perhaps believing he'd written it, the credit and royalties eventually went to Berry.
The listening guide compares the two.
Berry's version is at about 176 beats per minute, with uneven subdivisions, a strong backbeat, a guitar riff running through most of the song, and a boogie woogie piano solo with long glissandos.

Its sixteen bar verses are built from an antecedent phrase and a consequent phrase, two phrases on the same chords where the second sounds more final, and the band breaks for a solo voice in some verses.
The lyrics are about a sixteen year old girl begging her parents to let her go out to rock and roll, naming cities with good rock music.
It was number two pop for three weeks and number one rhythm and blues for three weeks.

Listen for the Four Freshmen style vocal harmonies, the imitation of Berry's guitar riff, and the organ and then guitar in the instrumental section.
items.lyr: A song about surfing and surfers. The singer wishes everyone in the country had an ocean and could have fun like the surfers in California, Australia, and Hawaii. Beach names take the place of the cities in Berry's song.
nl: The Beach Boys' version is a little slower, at about 164, with mostly even subdivisions, a strong backbeat, an imitation of Berry's guitar riff rhythm, and an organ and guitar solo.
Its antecedent and consequent phrases match Berry's closely, and the book suggests singing one of Berry's phrases followed by one of theirs to hear that Berry deserved the credit.
The lyrics wish that everyone in the country had an ocean, so they could surf like the surfers in California, Australia, and Hawaii, with surf spots replacing the cities in Berry's song.
It reached number three pop.

n: By late 1963, Brian Wilson had become a fine songwriter, expanding the group beyond beach songs to other teenage interests like school spirit and fast cars.
He also helped write and produce surf and car songs for his friends, the vocal duo Jan and Dean.
By 1966, Brian Wilson had a nervous breakdown and stopped touring, and his place on stage was taken first by Glen Campbell and then by Bruce Johnston.
First, Glen Campbell.
Bruce Johnston, with his early duo Bruce and Terry.
Free from touring, Brian kept writing, producing, singing, and playing on the records, and in 1966 he made the Beach Boys' most important album, Pet Sounds.
It wasn't their biggest seller, but all its songs were connected by a theme, and it sent rock albums in a new direction.
Concept albums existed before, but most rock albums were just collections of unrelated songs.
In Pet Sounds, the concept isn't even hinted at in the title, but emerges song by song: the hopes, dreams, and anxieties of a young person growing up.
Hopes appear in Wouldn't It Be Nice, Don't Talk, and I'm Waiting for the Day, and insecurity in I Know There's an Answer, I Just Wasn't Made for These Times, Caroline, No, and God Only Knows.
Its productions are thick, with many instrumental tracks layered on top of each other, much like Spector's wall of sound.
First, Wouldn't It Be Nice.

Caroline, No, the last song, followed by dogs barking and a passing train.
Pet Sounds may have started the concept album trend, but it was the Beatles' Sgt.
Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band, recorded the next year, that inspired other bands to make concept albums.
The Beatles quietly credited Pet Sounds by ending Good Morning Good Morning with animal sounds and a galloping horse, imitating the dogs and train at the end of Caroline, No.
Pet Sounds remains the Beach Boys' most important contribution to rock history because of its enormous influence.
To recap chapter five.
In the late fifties and early sixties, much of what was called rock and roll changed from the energetic blues and country based sound of the mid fifties to a gentler pop sound called teen idol pop.

This happened because established songwriters resented competition from rock musicians who wrote their own songs, because much rock was recorded on small labels hurt by the payola scandal, and because many parents objected to the rebellious, sexy lyrics and dances rooted in African American blues and rhythm and blues.
Teen pop was written for young teens, marketed through movies and radio, and often backed by orchestras instead of guitars, bass, and drums, with the backbeat largely gone.
By the early sixties, the West Coast surf style became popular: surf bands played their own instruments, but their songs were still lighthearted celebrations of youth.
The Beach Boys eventually left surf behind, creating complex studio productions like Spector's wall of sound.
